questions.q: Why isn't passing Lesson 4's image check, Lesson 5's VM check, and Lesson 6's alert check, each in isolation, the same as end-to-end testing?
options: It is the same -- no further testing is needed once each piece passes individually
The pieces could each work alone while failing together -- for example, a page loading fine but referencing a broken image URL, or an alert rule existing but being silently misconfigured
End-to-end testing is only required for applications with more than one VM
Isolated checks are always less reliable than end-to-end checks, regardless of what they test
questions.explain: Each isolated check passing doesn't guarantee the whole system behaves correctly together, the way a real customer or on-call engineer would actually experience it.

questions.q: Why does the checklist specifically say to browse at least three different product categories, not just one?
options: Azure requires testing at least three pages before considering a migration valid
To confirm the migration works across the catalog broadly, not just the one page someone happened to test first
Because each product category uses a different storage account
Three is an arbitrary number with no real reasoning behind it
questions.explain: Testing only the first page you happen to check risks missing a problem that only shows up elsewhere in the catalog.

questions.q: Why does the checklist insist on actually triggering the CPU alert with a real stress test, rather than just confirming the alert rule exists in Azure?
options: Because `az monitor metrics alert create` always fails silently
Because a command returning without an error only confirms the rule was created, not that it actually fires and notifies correctly when the real condition is met
Because Azure requires every alert rule to be manually triggered once before it becomes active
There's no real reason -- it's just good practice with no specific risk behind it
questions.explain: The same lesson as earlier in this course: a command finishing without an error doesn't prove the thing it configured actually works. Only a real trigger proves that.

questions.q: Why does the checklist also check that the alert resolves once CPU drops back under 80%, not just that it fires?
options: Resolution doesn't matter -- only firing matters
An alert that fires but never clears is its own configuration problem, just as real as one that never fires at all
Alerts automatically resolve after exactly 24 hours regardless of configuration
Resolution is only relevant for log-based alerts, not metric alerts
questions.explain: A stuck, permanently-firing alert is a real operational problem -- confirming it clears once the condition is no longer true is part of proving the alert actually works correctly.

questions.q: What is explicitly NOT part of this lesson's end-to-end checklist?
options: Confirming product images load from their new Blob Storage URLs
Checking the Activity Log for a clean resource history
Full launch-day load testing, security penetration testing, and disaster-recovery failover testing
Triggering the CPU alert and confirming it fires and later clears
questions.explain: This checklist covers correctness and basic reliability. Load testing at full launch-day traffic, security testing, and DR failover testing are real practices for a more mature platform, not this project's scope.
